ignored.text: The barrels keep rolling, and so do the rumours.

stages.text: {keeper} asks for a bell to hang at the foot of the stair, so that whatever tries to come up rings it before it reaches the street.

success.text: The bell is cast and hung. Twice that winter it rings in the night, and twice the watch is down there before it stops.
You find a place for the lantern where the whole stair can see it. It will do, nearly.

failure.text: {keeperName} hangs a lantern and says nothing more about it.

ignored.text: The warden hangs an old pot on a chain instead.

stages.text: A wild flight of griffons has come down from the peaks and is circling the roost, screaming. {keeper} says the tame ones want to join them, and the wild ones want the town's sheep.

options.label: Let the riders drive them off

success.text: The riders go up, and the wild flight goes back to the peaks with one fewer of its number.

failure.text: Two riders come down hurt, and the wild flight takes the sheep anyway.

success.text: A wild griffon lands on the roost and stays. The flight is one stronger.

failure.text: The wild griffon will not be tamed, and takes a rider's arm with it when it goes.

success.text: The wild flight eats well for a week and leaves. The shepherds are paid for their sheep.

ignored.text: The wild flight takes a dozen sheep and a shepherd's dog and goes.

stages.text: {hero}'s company wants to hire griffons to fly them over the worst of the road to their next job. {keeper2} thinks it is a fine idea; {keeper} says the griffons are not mules.

success.text: {heroName}'s company flies out over the trees, and is back before anyone expected.

failure.text: The griffons won't fly for strangers. Two riders go out with them, and one comes back hurt.

options.label: Lend one rider to scout for them

success.text: A rider scouts the road ahead and the company walks it safely.

failure.text: The rider's griffon goes lame on the second day, and the company walks the rest.

success.text: The company walks, grumbling, and the hall's clerks grumble louder.

ignored.text: The company walks.

stages.text: Something got out of the sanctuary overnight. {keeper} will not say what, only that it is probably not dangerous and that everyone should stay indoors.

options.label: Send the watch to hunt it

success.text: The watch corners a terrified mirage-lynx kitten in a bakery and brings it back in a sack.

failure.text: The watch corners it, and it was dangerous. Two of them are in the healers' house.

success.text: {keeperName} sits in the square with a bucket of eels and a lullaby, and by dawn it has crept back to its pen.

failure.text: It does not come back, and the bucket of eels is found empty in the morning.

options.label: Shut the sanctuary until it is found

success.text: The pens are closed and the town hunts it for a week.

ignored.text: It is found three days later living under the temple steps, and the town will not forget it.

stages.text: {hero} has come back from a ruin with a warm, humming egg. {keeper} would give a great deal to keep it, and admits not knowing what it will hatch into.

success.text: The egg is set in a nest of coals. The town lines up to look at it.

failure.text: The egg goes cold in its first night at the sanctuary. The keepers grieve; the town is uneasy.

success.text: A collector from the coast pays a fortune for it.

failure.text: The buyers smell how badly you want it gone, and pay accordingly.

success.text: {heroName} smashes it. Whatever was inside was very nearly something.

ignored.text: {heroName} keeps it under the bed, and the inn's rooms are warmer all winter.

stages.text: {keeper2} wants three of the sanctuary's beasts for the great games. {keeper} would sooner feed the Arena Master to them.

success.text: The games are the best in years, and one beast does not come back.

failure.text: A beast turns on its handler in the ring, and the sanctuary takes the rest home that night.

success.text: The games go on with hired brawlers. The crowds are thinner.

options.label: A show of tricks, not a fight

success.text: The beasts perform, untouched, and the crowd loves them more than any fight.

failure.text: The beasts will not perform, and the crowd jeers both keepers.

ignored.text: The Arena Master steals a beast in the night, and both keepers come to the council shouting.

stages.text: A merchant who bought a silver mirror at the auction house says it whispers at night and that his wife has started answering. He wants his money back. {keeper} says all sales are final.

success.text: {keeperName} refunds him with a face like a closed door. The mirror goes back in the vault.

failure.text: The house refunds him, and tells every buyer on the coast that {town}'s auctions are not final.

options.label: Have a priest break the curse

success.text: The mirror stops whispering. The merchant's wife misses it.

failure.text: The priest breaks the mirror, and the whispering moves into the walls.

success.text: The merchant leaves town, mirror and all.

ignored.text: The merchant's wife leaves town with the mirror, and he blames the council.

stages.text: Lot forty-two is a fine oak chest, and it has eaten an under-auctioneer. {keeper} would like to sell it anyway, as a curiosity.

success.text: A collector buys it at a fine price and is never seen again. Nor is the chest.

failure.text: It sells cheap, and eats a footman before it reaches the buyer's carriage.

success.text: The watch hacks it apart. It screams. Nobody in the hall sleeps well that night.

options.label: Lock it in an iron box

success.text: The chest goes into a lead-lined vault with the other things that knock. The auctioneer approves of the vault, if not the loss.

failure.text: It won't go in the box. The smith's apprentice loses a sleeve finding out, and the box goes back unused.

ignored.text: The chest wanders off one night and turns up in a tavern cellar.

stages.text: {keeper} has a holy relic up for sale, plundered from a ruined shrine. {keeper2} says it belongs to the gods and will not have it sold to the highest bidder.

success.text: The council buys the relic and gives it back to the gods. The temple is grateful, and so is the auctioneer.
The auctioneer gives it up and does not forgive the council.

failure.text: The house gives it up, and the buyers who were promised it never bid in {town} again.

success.text: A stranger in grey buys it, and the priests pray against him.

failure.text: It sells, and the temple names the buyer from the pulpit.

ignored.text: The relic is sold to a stranger and the priests preach against the auction house.

stages.text: {hero} has their eye on a black sword at the auction: fine steel, an old curse, and a reputation for making its owners great and then terrible. {keeper} says the bidding opens tomorrow.

success.text: {heroName} carries the black sword out of the hall. It fits their hand perfectly.
{heroName} lets it go, and the sword goes to a mercenary who is never heard of again.

failure.text: {heroName} buys it anyway, sulking.

options.label: Buy it and lock it away

success.text: The council buys the sword and puts it in the vault, where it waits.

ignored.text: {heroName} buys it while the council is still talking.

stages.text: A baker traded the colour of her eyes for a basket of fey bread that never goes stale. Now she wants her eyes back. {keeper} says a bargain is a bargain.

success.text: The baker keeps her bread and her grey eyes. The fey trade more freely with a town that keeps its word.

failure.text: The bargain is honoured, but the family cannot forgive the town for letting it stand.

success.text: The fey trader gives back the colour of her eyes in exchange for a song no one has heard before. The town's bards are busy for a week.

failure.text: The fey trader agrees, for the colour of the mayor's own eyes. The council declines.

success.text: The market stays, but the fey trade sourly now.

ignored.text: The baker sells fey bread for the rest of her life and never complains again.

stages.text: A family swears their baby was swapped for a changeling on market night. {keeper} says the fey would never; the family has a pitchfork.

success.text: It is their baby, teething and furious. The family is reassured, and the market's name with it.

failure.text: Nobody can tell, and the street divides over it.

options.label: Demand the fey return the child

success.text: The fey take the demand with a bow and return the child, though they won't trade with you for a while.

failure.text: The fey laugh at the demand, and the market sleeps badly for a month.

options.label: Close the market for a month

success.text: The stalls do not come back for a month, and the town is duller for it.

ignored.text: The family leaves town with a baby that laughs at things no one else can see.

requests.title: A fey road through the grove

stages.text: {keeper} wants to open a fey road from the market through the grove's oldest trees, so traders can come from the Hollow Hill directly. {keeper2} says the trees will never be the same.

success.text: Fey traders walk out of the oldest oak on market nights. The market thrives; the grove sulks.

failure.text: The road opens crooked. Travellers come through it lost and frightened, and the grove is furious.

success.text: The trees stay as they are, and the fey market's warden goes quiet.

options.label: Let the druids and the fey bargain

success.text: The druids set terms the fey can keep. The road opens on the solstice only.

failure.text: The druids and the fey quarrel, and the oak splits.

ignored.text: A fey road opens anyway, one night, and closes behind three townsfolk.

stages.text: {keeper} has seen a place in the smoke: {site}, and what waits there. She will describe it for the council's maps, for a price.

success.text: The oracle describes {site} in detail, and the cartographers draw it in.

options.label: Ask her to describe it for the good of the town

success.text: She describes it, sighing, and the maps are richer for it.

failure.text: She will not, and the vision fades.

success.text: You decline with a gift of incense, and she takes it gracefully.

failure.text: {keeperName} keeps the vision to herself, as is her right.

ignored.text: The vision fades, unrecorded.

stages.text: {keeper} has foretold that the town will burn before the year is out. The town is in a panic. She is quite sure, mostly.

success.text: The town digs firebreaks and fills cisterns. Nothing burns. Was the prophecy wrong, or was it averted?
She reads again: it was not the town that would burn, but a barn. The barn burns. Everyone is relieved.

failure.text: She reads again and sees it again. The town is more frightened than ever.

success.text: She goes quiet, and the town is spared the panic, though she will not read for you again soon.

failure.text: She won't be silenced. She cries the doom in the square instead, louder for being forbidden.

ignored.text: The prophecy spreads unchecked, and the town lives in fear.

stages.text: {keeper} needs the library's oldest star charts. {keeper2} will not let them leave the building.

success.text: The charts go to the tower. The oracle's readings grow sharper, and the librarian sulks.

failure.text: The librarians lend them, with an inventory as long as your arm and a complaint to the council.

options.label: Have the oracle read them in the library

success.text: The oracle reads them at the library's tables, and both keepers learn something.

failure.text: The oracle reads them under the librarians' eyes and sees nothing she trusts.

success.text: The oracle reads the sky without them, and says so often.

ignored.text: The charts stay in the library, and the oracle stops speaking to the librarian.

stages.text: A company went down the shaft four days ago with rope for three. {keeper} has heard nothing up the speaking tube since yesterday and wants a rescue sent before the lanterns run out.

success.text: {heroName} finds them on the sixth stair, starving behind a door that only opens from outside, and brings every one of them up.

failure.text: {heroName} brings up two of the five, and does not talk about the other three.

options.label: Lower the rescue rope and wait

success.text: On the third night a hand pulls on the rope. Then four more.

failure.text: The rope comes up cut.

success.text: {keeper} crosses their names off the ledger, slowly.

ignored.text: Nobody goes after them. Their names stay in the ledger with no line through them.

stages.text: A company has come up the shaft with a Stoneking's hoard: gold rings the size of cartwheels and a crown no one can lift alone. The town's charter says a share is the council's. {keeper} says the companies will stop coming if the council takes it.

success.text: The treasury fills. The next companies go down a little less eagerly.
The company drinks the town dry and tells everyone where they found it. More companies arrive.

failure.text: The company keeps every coin, and the council grumbles about the gold walked past its door.

options.label: Buy the crown for the town

success.text: The giant's crown is set up in the square. People sit in it.

failure.text: The company's price goes up halfway through the bargain. You pay it, and the town gets its crown.

ignored.text: The company sells the hoard piecemeal in the next town over.

stages.text: Something came up the shaft clinging under the winch cage and is now loose in the cellars round the Delve. {keeper} saw it go by and will only say it had too many joints.

options.label: Send the watch into the cellars

success.text: The watch corners it in a cooper's cellar and finishes it with pitchforks and spears.

failure.text: It takes a watchman before the rest drive it back down the shaft.

options.label: Have the Delvemaster lure it back

success.text: {keeperName} lowers a side of beef and the cage, and it climbs aboard. The cage goes down without it coming back.

failure.text: It takes the beef and stays.

options.label: Shut the Delve until it's found

success.text: A week of shut doors. A cat finds it first, and nobody is sure the cat won.

ignored.text: It is seen on rooftops for a month, then not again.

stages.text: On the ninth level {keeper}'s mappers found a giant's door carved with a map of the world above. One mark on it lies where no one in town has ever been: {site}.

success.text: {heroName} spends a night under the door with chalk and paper and comes up with a road to {site}.

failure.text: {heroName} copies half of it before the lantern fails.

success.text: It opens on a sealed vault, and the vault on a staircase going down again. The Delve is deeper than anyone thought.

failure.text: It does not open, and something on the other side knows someone tried.

success.text: The mappers are told to stop at eight. They grumble, and keep mapping.

ignored.text: The mappers copy the door on their own and sell the map in the tavern.

stages.text: {keeper2} wants every company that goes down the shaft registered at the hall and paying its dues there. {keeper} says the Delve keeps its own ledger and always has.

success.text: Contracts, dues and rescue insurance, all in the hall's neat hand. The Delvemaster sulks by the winch.

failure.text: The hall gets the ledger, and the Delve keeps a second one out of spite.

success.text: {keeperName} keeps the ledger. The Hallmaster keeps a list of grievances.

failure.text: The Delve keeps its ledger, and the hall's companies make a point of not signing it.

success.text: Two keepers and one ledger. They argue over every line and catch every mistake.

ignored.text: Two ledgers, neither complete, and a company goes down that is in neither.

stages.text: A company has brought up a pale, eyeless beast from the bottom of the Delve, alive, in a net. {keeper2} wants it for the sanctuary. {keeper} wants it thrown back down before its mother comes looking.

success.text: The beast settles in the sanctuary's darkest pen and eats only mushrooms. Scholars come from three towns.

failure.text: It settles in. Then, one night, something large comes up the shaft looking for it.

success.text: The net is lowered on the winch and comes up empty. The Delve is quiet.
A collector from the coast pays very well and asks no questions.

failure.text: The beast fetches little, and both houses think less of you for selling it.

ignored.text: The beast chews through the net and goes home on its own.

stages.text: The envoy from {settlement} asks for a lower toll on their wagons. {keeper} says it would make a friend of them; the merchants say it would make a beggar of the treasury.

success.text: {settlement}'s wagons roll in toll-free and their envoy toasts the town at every dinner.
{keeperName} trades the toll for {settlement}'s grain at a good price. Both sides call it a victory.

failure.text: The envoy takes offence at the haggling and goes home early.

success.text: You refuse, but offer a feast-day market in their name. It is not the toll, but it softens the blow.

failure.text: The envoy bows very low and very coldly.

ignored.text: The envoy waits a month for an answer, then stops waiting.

stages.text: Two envoys both claim the same corner of the square for their banners, and one has challenged the other to a duel at dawn. {keeper} begs the council to stop it without seeming to take sides.

success.text: Both envoys are seated at the council's table, with the fountain between them. By the pudding they are allies against the cook.
They duel at dawn with a healer standing by. First blood, and both go home with their honour.

failure.text: The duel goes too far and the healer comes too late to keep it quiet. Both houses blame the town.

options.label: Settle it by the old charter

success.text: {keeper} finds a line in the charter that gives the corner to neither. Both are equally annoyed, which is the point.

failure.text: The charter is no help, and both envoys say so to their kings.

ignored.text: They duel. Nobody dies, but their kings hear about it.

stages.text: A minor noble has climbed the embassy quarter's wall at night and asks the town for sanctuary from their own family. {keeper} says hiding them will be noticed, and handing them over will be remembered.

success.text: You grant sanctuary and talk the embassy round to calling it a kindness to both.

failure.text: Sanctuary is granted, and the embassy treats it as an act of war in every letter home.

success.text: The family sends a gift of thanks and a promise. The noble's servants spit as they pass the town hall.
The family wanted them married to a lich's grandson. The town keeps them, and nobody argues.

failure.text: The story changes every time they tell it.

ignored.text: The noble climbs back over the wall and is gone by morning.

stages.text: Three envoys have been drinking in {keeper2}'s back room every night and talking far too freely. {keeper} wants it stopped; {keeper2} says it is the best trade the tavern has had all year.

success.text: The tavern's ears and the council's purse both do well. The envoys never suspect.

failure.text: The envoys spot your listener on the second night, and the tavern loses them for good.

options.label: Give the envoys their own cellar

success.text: The quarter gets a wine cellar of its own. The tavern loses its best customers.
The envoys are touched by the warning and drink more carefully, and more gratefully.

failure.text: The envoys take the warning as a threat, and the tavern takes it as a betrayal.

ignored.text: One envoy says something unforgivable about another's queen, loudly.

stages.text: The elven envoys want the grove's druids to sing a pavilion of living trees into the embassy square. {keeper2} will do it if the square's paving comes up for good. {keeper} hates the idea of mud at a reception.

success.text: The pavilion grows overnight, boughs knotted into a roof. Envoys sign under it and seem to mean it.
A handsome pavilion of potted trees. The elves are too polite to say what they think.

failure.text: The trees sicken in their tubs within the month, and the druids say so to everyone.

success.text: The paving stays. The elven envoy plants one seed between two stones anyway.

failure.text: The envoys get their paving, and the grove takes it as the town's answer to it.

ignored.text: A tree comes up through the paving on its own, and nobody quite dares cut it down.

requests.title: A treaty that must be sung

stages.text: A merchant delegation has come through the ring from a place where every agreement must be sung, and refuses to sign anything spoken. {keeper} needs someone to sing the town's side of the deal.

success.text: Your voice cracks on the third verse, and the delegation weeps for joy at your sincerity. The deal is very good.

failure.text: The delegation listens politely, then sings a short, sad verse about tone.

success.text: The choir sings the terms in four parts. The delegation signs, and asks for the choir's names.
You send them home with gifts and a promise of a song next time. They take it graciously.

failure.text: They sing their farewell on the way back through the ring. It is quite rude.

ignored.text: The delegation sings to the square all night, then leaves.

stages.text: The ring flared at midnight and something stepped through that nobody had tuned it for. It is sitting in the gatehouse yard, very still, looking at the town. {keeper} has the ring shut and wants orders.

success.text: It was lost, and grateful, and leaves a gift of something warm and bright before it goes back.

failure.text: It answers in a way that makes the watch's noses bleed, and walks back through the ring. Nobody sleeps that night.

options.label: Drive it back with the watch

success.text: The watch advances in a line, and it steps backwards through the ring with what looks like a shrug.

failure.text: The watch advances, and two of them do not come back from the far side of the ring.

success.text: By dawn it is gone. So are all the town's bells.

ignored.text: It walks into the town at dawn and is seen in three places at once.

stages.text: The black stones of the ring have begun to hum out of tune, and the far side flickers between places nobody chose. {keeper} says the ring needs costly re-attuning, or it should be shut for a season.

success.text: A week of chanting, chalk and silver dust, and the ring opens clean again.
The ring goes dark and the gatehouse yard goes quiet. Traders grumble.

failure.text: Shutting it is harder than opening it. The masons take twice as long, and the bill doubles.

options.label: Try to tune it by ear

success.text: {keeperName} hums at the stones for a day and a night, and they hum back in tune.

failure.text: The ring opens on somewhere very cold for an hour, and half the town has frostbite.

ignored.text: The ring opens itself one night onto a field of red grass, and closes again with three sheep from it in the yard.

stages.text: {keeper} wants the bards' college to write the town a treaty-song for the far side of the ring, so the town need not hire a choir each time. {keeper2} says a song like that is a year's work, and should be paid like it.

success.text: The college writes a treaty-song in nine verses, and the far side's merchants hum it on the way home. A stone from their city comes back as thanks.
Four verses, cheaply done. The far side finds it charming, in a provincial way.

failure.text: The short one is very short, and very bad. Nobody sings it twice.

success.text: No song, but you make it up to both with a toast in the square. They grumble, but go home.

failure.text: The gate keeps hiring choirs, and the college keeps not writing.

ignored.text: A student at the college writes one anyway and sells it to the gatehouse for a song.

requests.title: A visitor from the Hall of Hours

stages.text: A tall, quiet figure in white came through the ring and has been standing in the temple courtyard since dawn. {keeper2} thinks it is a messenger of the gods. {keeper} thinks it is a tourist.

success.text: It blesses the temple's bells, so that they ring true for a hundred years, and leaves without a word.

failure.text: It looks around the temple, sighs, and leaves.

success.text: It wanted to hear the town's bells. It hears them, smiles, and goes home.

failure.text: It answers in riddles, and the temple calls it a demon to the whole square.

success.text: It moves along, through the ring, without looking back. The priests are scandalised.

ignored.text: It stands in the courtyard for a week, then is gone, and the courtyard's flowers bloom out of season.

stages.text: {keeper} has found a letter in the founders' chest: the town's founding banner was carried off by raiders a lifetime ago and hung in a robber-lord's hall in the hills. The hall still stands. {keeper} asks for a hero to bring it home.

success.text: {heroName} finds the robber-lord's hall, and the banner in it, behind a robber-lord's grandson who wants a price.

failure.text: {heroName} finds the hall burned and the trail cold, for now.

success.text: A reward is cried in every town on the road. Months later, a pedlar brings a letter: the banner is in a robber-lord's hall, and its keeper wants a price.
{keeper} puts the letter back in the chest.

stages.text: The robber-lord's grandson will give the banner up for two hundred gold, or for a duel with the town's champion. {heroName} is ready either way.

success.text: The banner comes home in a cart, the whole town lining the road. It goes up over the empty pedestal.
{heroName} wins in the third pass and carries the banner home on their spear. The town will tell it for a hundred years.

failure.text: {heroName} loses, honourably, and comes home bloodied and empty-handed.

success.text: You walk away, and make the hall see it was the price, not the banner, that you refused.

failure.text: The banner stays in the hills. {keeper} sets the letter on the empty pedestal.

ignored.text: The letter goes back in the chest.

requests.title: An old hero wants to put down the sword

stages.text: {heroName} has been coming to the hall of heroes every evening to look at the old shields. {keeper} says they would make a fine teacher in the yard, if the town can spare them from the road.

success.text: {heroName} hangs up their sword in the hall and starts shouting at young heroes in the yard. The young heroes improve.

options.label: Ask them for one more season

success.text: {heroName} nods, and goes back out on the road. They still come to the hall every evening.

failure.text: {heroName} stays, but sourly, and the hall knows it.

success.text: {heroName} teaches in the yard when they are home, and the hall pays them for it.

failure.text: They teach, after a fashion: three lessons, then they're off on a contract again.

ignored.text: {heroName} keeps coming to the hall, and keeps saying nothing.

stages.text: {keeper} wants {fallen}'s shield hung in the hall of heroes and their name carved where the town will see it. The stonecutters want paying.

options.label: Carve the name and hang the shield

success.text: {fallen}'s shield goes up, and their name is the first on a new wall. People leave flowers under it.
The shield goes up on a nail by the door. {keeper} polishes it every day.

failure.text: The shield goes up, but the hall says a hero deserves their name too.

success.text: You promise the stone for spring, and mean it. The hall believes you, for now.

failure.text: {keeper} keeps the shield behind the counter.

ignored.text: The shield gathers dust behind the counter.

stages.text: A stranger in a travelling cloak says the great axe in the hall's third case belonged to their grandmother, and was lost at {site}. They will trade a map of the place for it. {keeper} would rather keep the axe.

options.label: Trade the axe for the map

success.text: The stranger leaves with the axe, crying. The map is very good.
The stranger leaves without it, and without leaving the map.

failure.text: You keep the axe, and the claimant tells every company on the road that {town} robbed them.

success.text: They know the name scratched under the axe's grip. {keeper} gives it back gladly, and they give the map gladly too.

failure.text: They cannot name the mark under the grip, and leave in a hurry.

ignored.text: The stranger comes back every week to look at the axe.

stages.text: {keeper2} has a battered shield on the block that {keeper} swears belonged to one of the town's founders. The auction house will not lower the reserve for sentiment.

success.text: The founder's shield goes up in the hall of heroes, and the auctioneer's commission goes up on the next lot.

options.label: Ask the auction house to donate it

success.text: {keeper2} gives it up with a speech about civic virtue, and charges the next three buyers more.

failure.text: {keeper2} laughs and sells it to a collector from the coast.

success.text: It sells, but you get the buyer to lend it to the hall on feast days.

failure.text: A collector from the coast buys it. {keeper} does not speak to {keeper2} for a month.

ignored.text: The shield sells while the council is still deciding.

stages.text: Sheep have been going missing from the hill farms, three at a time. {keeper} says, with great dignity, that the treaty's meat ration was set when it was smaller.

success.text: A cart of meat goes up the hill every day. The farms keep their sheep, and the treasury feels it.
It hunts the hills beyond the roads, and the wolves and worse that lived there are fewer.

failure.text: It hunts the wilds, and a drover's herd with them. The roads are emptier for a month.

success.text: {keeperName} hears the treaty read aloud, slowly, and agrees. The sheep stop going missing.

failure.text: {keeperName} hears the treaty read, and eats the parchment.

ignored.text: More sheep go missing, and then a cow, and then a barn.

stages.text: {keeper} has decided that its collection needs a piece from every great house in the town: a ring, a cup, a portrait. It asks the council to arrange it, as a courtesy.

options.label: Pay the tithe from the treasury

success.text: The council buys the pieces and sends them up the hill on velvet. {keeperName} is gracious about it for weeks.
Most houses give something small and showy. One gives nothing, and the dragon notices.

failure.text: The houses give, but every door you knock on remembers it.

success.text: You offer the dragon a seat at every feast instead. It is, it turns out, very lonely.

failure.text: It considers the offer, and declines it, and takes a weathervane on the way home.

ignored.text: Small things start to go missing from the great houses. Everyone knows where they went.

stages.text: {keeper} has flown over {settlement} and seen raiders closing on it. It asks the town to open its gates to their people, and says it will guard the road while they come.

success.text: A long column comes down the road under the dragon's wings. The town is crowded, and kinder.

failure.text: The gates open, but the town wants to know why its grain is feeding strangers.

success.text: Wagons of grain go out under the dragon's guard. {settlement} holds.
You send word and a cart of tools instead. It isn't much, but it isn't nothing.

failure.text: {keeperName} goes to guard them anyway, alone, and is gone a week.

ignored.text: The dragon guards {settlement} without the town, and comes back with opinions about it.

stages.text: {keeper} wants to read the library's oldest book: a chronicle of the giant kings. {keeper2} is afraid it will not give the book back, and more afraid of saying so.

success.text: It returns the book a month later, with notes in the margin in a script no one has seen for four thousand years. The scholars weep.

failure.text: The dragon borrows it, and the librarians count every day until it comes back singed.

options.label: Let it read in the library

success.text: The dragon lies in the courtyard with its head through the reading-room window, turning pages with a claw.
You refuse, but offer to have the passages copied out. The dragon is mollified, nearly.

failure.text: The dragon takes the refusal badly, and the librarians sleep with buckets of sand by their beds.

ignored.text: The book is found on the dragon's tower one morning, carefully returned the next.

stages.text: {keeper} has smelled the dragon's egg in {keeper2}'s care, and wants it. Whether as a parent, a guardian or a meal, it will not say.

success.text: The dragon carries the egg to its tower and broods it with great tenderness. The beastwarden is heartbroken.

failure.text: The dragon takes the egg, and the sanctuary keepers weep in the street.

success.text: Dragon and beastwarden sit up together through the hatching. Neither will say who cried.

failure.text: They quarrel over the egg, and the sanctuary loses a wall.

success.text: {keeper2} keeps the egg. The dragon circles the sanctuary every night, low.

ignored.text: The egg is gone from the sanctuary one morning. Nobody asks where.

stages.text: The griffons will not fly when the dragon is in the sky, and the dragon likes the sky at dawn. {keeper2} wants the dragon kept to its tower until noon. {keeper} finds the request impertinent.

success.text: Dragon at dawn, griffons at noon. Both keepers grumble and both keep to it.

failure.text: Nobody keeps to the hours. There are near misses over the market every morning.

success.text: The dragon keeps to its tower till noon, and lets everyone know it.
The roost flies at night now, and the riders are tired.

failure.text: You side with the dragon, and the roost's riders call it cowardice to your face.

ignored.text: A griffon and the dragon meet over the market at dawn. Nobody is hurt, but the market is.

stages.text: A clutch of griffon eggs rescued from poachers has hatched at the sanctuary. {keeper} wants to raise them wild and release them; {keeper2} wants them for a rescue flight to pull lost companies and caravans out of trouble.

success.text: The hatchlings grow up between the sanctuary and the roost, and fly rescue for the whole road.

failure.text: The hatchlings won't take the bit. They are neither wild nor tame, and both houses blame the other.

success.text: The young griffons are flown out to the hills and let go. One comes back every spring to look.
Two go to the roost, three go to the hills. Neither keeper is quite satisfied.

failure.text: The two halves won't be parted, and the whole brood ends up neither one thing nor the other.

ignored.text: The hatchlings grow up in the sanctuary, too tame for the wild and too wild for the roost.
